To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of an ongoing VAS display improves ED pain care.
the use of ongoing visual analog score (VAS) determination and display of the information to physicians at the head of emergency department (ED) beds improves patient pain care in the ED.
“Ongoing visual analog pain assessment and display in the Emergency Department improves pain management.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an effective method to improve pain care in the ED, a setting where pain is often undertreated.
the use of visual analog scales (VAS) in the assessment of pain in patients in an Emergency Department.
the development and testing of an electronic system for pain assessment and display in the Emergency Department (ED), and its effects on ED patient pain care.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a visual analog scale score displayed on a graph at the head of an Emergency Department bed is a more effective method of assessing pain than a visual analog scale charted in an ED patient chart.
ongoing VAS assessment with display of information at the bedside is a feasible method to improve pain management in an ED.
ongoing pain scores, when graphed, improve ED pain care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ongoing pain assessment with visual display of VAS scores is superior to tabulation of VAS scores in the ED chart for improving pain care.
the Graph group had better pain assessment and pain care than the Control and Tabulation groups.
ongoing pain score display in the emergency department improves pain care.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the display of VAS data on the wall of an ED room can improve pain assessment and care.
the ongoing visual analog score display is a useful adjunct in ED pain management and can help improve pain care.
ongoing VAS determination and display in the ED is feasible and may improve pain management.
